opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting moment, because scaling has kind of reshuffled the priorities for a lot of people, including me. A few years ago, a lot of research energy went into clever architectural tweaks or new inductive biases that would give you a couple of points on a benchmark. And what we've learned, sometimes painfully, is that a lot of those gains wash out once you scale up the data and the compute. So there's a natural question of: what kinds of research are actually robust to scale, and what kinds are going to be made obsolete by the next, bigger model?

For me, that's pushed my interest toward questions that become *more* relevant as models get bigger rather than less. One is understanding: what are these models actually learning, and how are they doing it? When a model can suddenly do something like multi-step arithmetic or follow a chain of reasoning, I want to know whether it's learned a general algorithm or whether it's pattern-matching in a way that'll break the moment you go slightly out of distribution. That's where things like length generalization and algorithmic reasoning get really interesting, because they're places where scale alone doesn't seem to fully solve the problem, and how you present the task, or how you prompt the model, can matter enormously.

Another shift is that the model itself has become something you study almost like a natural phenomenon. Instead of only asking "how do I design a better model," you also ask "given this enormously capable artifact, how do I elicit what it knows, steer it, and understand its failure modes?" In-context learning is a great example. Nobody really designed it in, it emerged, and now there's a whole research agenda around what it is and how to use it well.

And I'd add that scaling changes who can do what kind of research. If you're in academia, you're probably not going to train the next frontier model, so you have to think carefully about where you have comparative advantage. I think that's actually pushed a lot of people toward more scientific questions: careful, controlled experiments, often on smaller models or synthetic tasks, that tell you something general about how learning works. Those insights can transfer up, even if you can't run the giant experiment yourself.

So I don't think scaling makes research less interesting, it just changes the bar. The question I try to ask is: if someone scales this up 10x next year, does my result still matter? If the answer's yes, it's probably worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response says some benchmark gains wash out at scale and asks which research remains useful, but it does not identify scaling away model failures as a reason to deprioritize work fixing them.

r002.rationale: It describes research priorities shifting and the bar changing, but does not say large-model success is narrowing the range of questions considered interesting.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare diverse exploration favorably with convergence on similar research directions.

r004.rationale: The response discusses algorithmic reasoning and length generalization, but does not suggest compositionality will emerge through scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think scaling has reshuffled the priorities in a pretty profound way, and honestly it's made me rethink what I personally want to work on.

For a long time, a lot of the field, myself included, was oriented around clever ideas. You'd propose a new architecture, a new regularizer, a new inductive bias, show it beat the baseline on a benchmark, and that was a contribution. What scaling has shown is that a huge fraction of those contributions wash out once you have enough data and compute. The bitter lesson, basically. So the first-order effect is that the bar for "is this idea actually going to matter" has gone way up. If your method only helps at small scale, people are rightly skeptical.

But I don't think that means there's less interesting research to do. I think it shifts the questions. A few things feel more worth pursuing now than they did before.

One is understanding. We have these systems that work far better than we can explain, and the gap between capability and understanding keeps widening. Questions like what is actually being learned, why do certain abilities seem to emerge at scale, what's going on inside the network when it does in-context learning or follows an instruction. Those were somewhat niche questions before. Now they feel central, partly because they matter for safety and partly because, scientifically, it's embarrassing to have built something you can't explain.

Another is the question of what you can't get from scaling alone. There's been a lot of hype, and some of it is deserved, but there are still clear failure modes. Models that can't reliably execute an algorithm they've seen a thousand times, or that fall apart on slightly longer or slightly out-of-distribution versions of a task. I find that genuinely interesting because it tells you something about the nature of what these models learn, that it's maybe more like a very rich set of patterns than a set of composable procedures. Figuring out where that boundary is, and whether it's a data problem, a training objective problem, or something more fundamental, seems important.

And then there's a whole category of questions around how to work with these models rather than just train them. Prompting, teaching models to use tools, getting them to reason step by step. Some of that looks like engineering, but I think there's real science in it. If you think of the model as a kind of general learner, then the question of how you teach it, what the right curriculum or instruction looks like, is a research question, and it's one that's only possible because of scale.

The thing I try to be honest about is that there's a resource asymmetry now. Most academic labs can't train frontier models, so if your research program depends on that, you're in trouble. But I actually think the smartest response isn't to try to compete on scale. It's to ask the questions that the big labs don't have the incentive or the patience to ask carefully. Controlled experiments, small-scale studies that isolate a phenomenon, theory that explains something the empirical results only hint at. That work has arguably gotten more valuable, not less, because there's so much more to explain.

r001.rationale: The response says many contributions wash out at scale, but it does not identify scaling away model failures as a reason research to fix those failures may become less impactful. It instead describes failure modes that remain.

r002.rationale: The response says scaling reshuffles priorities and raises the bar for ideas, but it does not clearly say that scaling narrows the range of research questions considered interesting.

r003.rationale: The response endorses several research areas, but it does not compare diverse exploration favorably with convergence on similar directions.

r004.rationale: The response questions whether models learn composable procedures and asks what cannot be obtained from scaling alone; it does not suggest compositionality will probably emerge through scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes what we consider a convincing result. If you propose a new method, you have to ask whether the improvement comes from that method, or whether you could get the same improvement by making the baseline bigger or training it longer. That’s a useful discipline, because it forces us to be clearer about what our contributions actually are.

But I think there’s a risk of taking that too far and deciding that the only question worth pursuing is how to scale things up. There’s a difference between knowing that something works and understanding why it works. The success of large models makes some of those questions more interesting: what are they learning, why do particular capabilities emerge, and when should we expect them to fail?

It also affects who can work on which questions. If a research direction requires training the largest model, very few groups can participate. So I think it’s valuable to find questions where a carefully designed experiment can teach us something, even at a smaller scale, while being honest about whether that conclusion carries over. Scaling gives us a very strong baseline, but I wouldn’t want it to become the sole criterion for deciding what’s worth understanding.

r001.rationale: The response questions making scaling the only research focus, but does not say that scaling away model failures makes research to fix those failures less impactful.

r002.rationale: It warns that researchers may decide “the only question worth pursuing” is scaling, describing a narrowing of which questions seem worth pursuing.

r003.rationale: It supports studying questions that can be addressed at smaller scales, but does not clearly prefer exploring diverse ideas over converging on similar research directions.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention compositionality or predict that it will emerge through scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling has changed the baseline for what counts as an interesting result. If a fairly general method keeps getting better with more data and compute, then, when you propose something more complicated, you have to ask: is this actually giving us something that scaling wouldn’t give us anyway? That’s a useful question, although it can make it harder to justify exploring ideas whose benefits aren’t immediately visible at scale.

But I don’t think the conclusion should be that all the interesting questions are now about making models bigger. There’s still a lot we don’t understand about why these methods work, what they learn, and when they fail. A model can perform very well without us having a good explanation of how it arrived at that behavior.

So I’d distinguish between scaling as a way to improve performance and scaling as an explanation. It’s been tremendously successful at the first. That success gives us new phenomena to study, but it doesn’t, by itself, answer the scientific questions. To me, that makes understanding learning more interesting, even if the incentives sometimes push toward just demonstrating the next performance improvement.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling can make it harder to justify complicated methods or ideas with benefits that are not immediately visible. It does not identify model failures being scaled away as the reason research to fix them may become less impactful.

r002.rationale: It says scaling has changed what counts as interesting and made it harder to justify exploring ideas whose benefits are not immediately visible at scale, describing pressure that narrows which questions seem worthwhile.

r003.rationale: The response argues that understanding learning remains interesting despite incentives to demonstrate performance gains. It does not clearly say that exploring diverse ideas is preferable to converging on similar research directions.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention compositionality or suggest it will emerge through scaling.
